note:
1911 household schedules supplied by A. Hagues, filling the second half of the gaps the census-gap report found - the streets the record holds in 1891 and again in 1921 but not in 1901 or 1911.

**These are the householder's own schedules, not the enumerator's book.** The hand is the head of the household's, the signature at the foot is his, and the 1911 return asks a woman three questions no earlier census did: how long she has been married, how many children she has borne, and how many are still living. Those answers are kept here because nothing else in the record can supply them.

**Not named people_*.json on purpose**, so the importer never reads it. A reading I am unsure of carries [?].
source: 1911 census household schedules - transcribed by Claude from images supplied by A. Hagues

marriage.note: Married about 1878. The four are Harold (1879), Oswald (1882), Dorothea (1884) and Ursula (1891), and in 1911 all four were alive.

people.name: John Kenneth Varvill
people.note: Entered first as NEPHEW, struck through and altered to Visitor in the same hand.

households.note: Fills the 1911 half of the gap at 9 Newcastle Drive. The record holds John (#2128), Jessie (#2129) and Ursula in 1891 and again in 1921, so this is the middle of a run of at least thirty years in one house - the longest single tenure the gap report turned up on that street.

**THE GAP REPORT READ THIS AS TWO CHANGES OF FAMILY, AND IT IS ONE MAN MOVING HOUSE.** William Thomas Cartwright is at **1 Newcastle Drive** in 1891 and at **7** in 1901, 1911 and 1921. The report showed 1 Newcastle Drive as Cartwright-to-Copeland and 7 as Birkin-to-Cartwright, because it compares each house with itself and cannot see a household walk down its own street. His daughter Margaret Helen (#2153) carries both ends - 1891 at number 1, 1921 at number 7.

Mary J. Cartwright, his wife, is alive in 1901 and he is a widower here, so she died between the two returns. Vincent Henry (#1781, born 1883) is already in the record, at 2 Park Ravine by 1921.

people.name: Charlotte Loder
people.note: "Coachman" was written in her occupation column and struck out - her husband's trade carried down a line by mistake.

people.name: Stanley Loder
people.note: Charlotte gives three children in twenty-six years and she is 54, so an infant of eighteen months is very unlikely to be hers. A grandson, with the relationship column left blank.

households.note:
**SETTLED BY THE SCHEDULE COVER: *Back of 5 Newcastle Drive, The Park, Nottingham*.** The enumerator first wrote *Huntingdon Drive, The Park*, struck it through, and wrote the back of 5 underneath. So this is the coach house or stable flat behind **5 Newcastle Drive (#210)**, and A. Hagues had it right.

**My reasoning against it was worthless.** I argued from the schedule numbers - 14 at number 7, 18 at number 9, so 17 must fall between them - and an enumerator numbering back premises does not walk in a straight line. An address written on the paper beats an inference from the order of the paper every time.

**And the big house ties the two together.** 5 Newcastle Drive on the same night is Henry Gee's, and one of his four servants is **Fanny Charlotte Loder**, housemaid, 24, born Nottingham. Charles and Charlotte Loder are at the back with a son of 16. Fanny Charlotte is almost certainly their daughter: the coachman drives for the house, his wife keeps the coach house, and his daughter is in service in the front of the same property.

**Charlotte reports three children born alive and three still living.** Charles Wood, 16, and Fanny Charlotte, 24, are two of them. The third is elsewhere. Stanley, eighteen months, is not one of the three, so he is a generation down - whose is not on the paper.

people.name: Fanny Charlotte Loder
people.note: Almost certainly the daughter of Charles and Charlotte Loder at the back of this same house - schedule 17.

households.note:
Closes the 1911 half of the gap at 5 Newcastle Drive. The record holds **Thomas Hill**, hosiery manufacturer, there in 1891 and again in 1901 at 78 and widowed - and **Henry Gee** there in 1921. This puts Gee in the house by 1911, so the handover happened in that decade, and one hosiery manufacturer followed another into it.

Clara married about 1871 and bore two children, both living in 1911. Neither is in the house.

The cover gives the district numbers for the whole round: registration district 430, sub-district 1, **enumeration district 11** - which is the district to ask for if the rest of this 1911 round is wanted.

people.name: Mary Elizabeth Patterson
people.note: The record holds her as **Mary ELY Patterson**. This return writes it out as Elizabeth, and A. Hagues confirms it. Ely is a misreading of an abbreviated Elizth.

people.name: Emma Jarvis
people.note: The index reads the birthplace as "Bowns"; the record has Bourne from both 1891 and 1901, so Bourne it is.

people.name: Dora Muffel
people.note: The index reads "Manla Cambs". Manea is a Cambridgeshire village and the likeliest reading, but it is a guess at one letter and is marked as one.

households.note:
Closes the 1911 half of the gap at 1 Park Terrace. The record holds Mary Patterson there in 1891 and 1901 and a different family, the Cockburns, by 1921 - so this is the last census of her tenancy, at 82 and still keeping two servants.

**Emma Jarvis has been with her at least twenty years.** She is a servant in this house in 1891 at 31, in 1901 at 46 and here in 1911 at 51 - one woman across three returns, with the ages drifting as census ages do.

**And she is in the record twice because of that drift.** #3585 carries her 1891 row at born 1860; #4757 was created by the 1901 gap-round import at born 1855, because the page gave her age as 46. Five years apart, so neither the duplicates page nor variant_duplicates.py can see them - both test born years within two. This return gives 51, which agrees with #3585, so #3585 is the one to keep.

people.name: Kate Reid
people.note: **Kate Elizabeth Reid (#1789).** The record has her at 6 Park Terrace in 1901 as the sister-in-law of William H. Foster - I transcribed that page as *Kate E. Reis* - and back at 2 Park Terrace as head in 1921. Married twenty years and widowed by 1911, with no children born to the marriage.

people.name: Frances Mary Wing
people.note: **Almost certainly Frances May KING (#1790) of the 1921 return** - same house, same birth year, same birthplace, and a second Head beside Kate Reid there in 1921 just as she is Joint Tenant here. King for Wing and May for Mary: two single-letter misreadings in one name. She is also very likely the Frances Wing, 36, who is Henry Wing's daughter at 12 Park Terrace on the 1901 round.

households.note:
Closes the 1911 half of the gap at 2 Park Terrace, and it is not a family at all: two women of independent means keeping house together, one a widow and one a spinster, entered as **Head and Joint Tenant**. The record has the same pair there in 1921, where the transcription made them two Heads.

**"Joint Tenant" is a relationship the record has nowhere else.** It is worth keeping as the page wrote it rather than flattening it to lodger or boarder, because it says something the other words do not: neither woman was the other's dependant.

**And it settles the Wellington question.** Kate Reid was genuinely born at Wellington, New Zealand, so the record's two rows under that place are right. The record also holds one *Wellington, Somerset*, which is a different place and a different person.

people.name: Herbert Bradley
people.note: **#1796.** This is the fourth census of him the record now holds: a boarder at 10 Park Terrace in 1891, head of number 3 in 1901, here in 1911, still there in 1921. He was the anchor picked for searching this street and he has turned out to span it.

people.name: Mary Saxby
people.note: **Recorded as 45 in 1901 AND 45 here, ten years apart**, and the record holds two Mary Saxbys at this house - #4760 born 1856 from the 1901 round and #1797 Mary E Saxby born 1861 from 1921. Three birth years and three birthplaces (Somercotes, Derby, Southwell) for one servant in one house. Almost certainly one woman; not bound to either number here, because which is the keeper is not something this page can settle.

households.note: Closes the 1911 half of the gap at 3 Park Terrace. Eight rooms, three people, and the householder's own signature at the foot.

A household entirely new to the record, and entirely Cornish. **Four of the five Thomases were born at St Michael's Mount** - a tidal island of a few dozen souls - and their widowed mother a little inland. A dentist of 35 keeping house with his mother and three unmarried sisters, three hundred miles from where all of them were born.

1901 held Herbert Lancashire, hosiery manufacturer, so the house changed hands entirely in the decade.

people.name: Annie May
people.note: Entered as Single with "Widow" struck through - the householder changed his mind about her.

households.note: **9 Park Terrace is usually empty, and this is the only household the record will hold for it.** It was returned uninhabited in 1901, holds two people in 1891 and nobody at all in 1921. Here a newly married couple - the marriage under a year old and no children - with a cook and a housemaid.

people.name: John Henry Runge
people.occupation: Secretary in a limited liability company, lace
people.note: **Born in Germany and naturalised in 1875**, which the schedule states outright. The record has him as a naturalised British subject from the 1891 return but not the year.

households.note:
**This is the house he moved to, and it closes the Park Valley question.** The record holds John Henry Runge at 17 Park Valley in 1891 and at 10 Park Terrace in 1921; the gap report could only say a Runge had gone from one and arrived at the other. He is here in 1911, so the move happened between 1901 and 1911 - and 17 Park Valley already held William Ranson, physician, by 1901.

**And the 1911 questions say something no other return could.** Married forty years, **one child born alive, none still living, one died**. A marriage of forty years and a single child who did not survive - a fact the record could not have held before, because only the 1911 census asked.

**A woman heads this house and she is a head mistress** - the only one the record holds. She keeps a housekeeper and takes a boarder, a young assistant dental surgeon from Cheshire. Three people, all single, none related to each other.

Her surname is read here as Nicolls and her employer as the Midland Institute; both are uncertain in the hand. 1901 held Richard Beaumont, solicitor, so the house turned over entirely.

people.name: Charles Edward Townroe
people.note: The hand is hard and an index may read the surname as Tannoc. It is Townroe: the same forenames, the same rare middle name in his wife, the same trade and the same town.

people.name: Mary Dakeyne Townroe
people.note: **The record spells her Daykene**, from the 1891 return. Her husband writes it **Dakeyne** here in his own hand, which is the better authority.

households.note:
**THE TOWNROES, AND THIS IS WHERE THEY WENT.** The record holds Charles Edward and Mary at **2 Lenton Road** in 1891, and A. Hagues's reading of the 1901 round put them still there under the hand's *Tomnroe*. Here they are at 12 Park Terrace in 1911 - the same couple, the bank clerk and his wife, one street over.

**And the marriage questions account for the children.** Married twenty-seven years, so about 1884: **three born alive, two still living, one died**. The record holds Bernard Stephen (1885) and Sybil Mary (1889) from 1891 and Geoffrey C. (1895) from 1901 - three children, and one of them did not live.

people.name: Frederic Dunnill
people.occupation: Organist and teacher of music | Own account

households.note:
**An organist and teacher of music**, working on his own account - the second musical household the record has found on the estate, after the Horners, father and son, both professors of music at Oakleigh on Hamilton Drive in 1901.

Newly married, under a year, and no children. 1901 held Richard Beaumont, solicitor, with one housekeeper.

people.name: Tinsley Lindley
people.note: **#1819.** The record holds him at this house in 1901 and 1921 and as **Tinster Lindey** in the 1921 transcription. He signs this schedule himself: **Tinsley Lindley**.

people.name: Constance A. Lindley
people.note: **The record holds her twice and neither is right.** #1820 *Constance Agnes Lindey* from 1921 has the forename but not the surname; #4785 *Constance Lindley* from the 1901 round has the surname but not the forename. Her age here agrees with #1820.

households.note:
**Tinsley Lindley in his own hand.** He is in the record at this house across three censuses and is not marked as a notable resident, which on the face of the record is reasonable - a barrister of 45. He was also an England footballer, and worth looking into before the record settles on calling him a lawyer.

**And the marriage answers close his family.** Married fifteen years, so about 1896: **one child born alive, one still living**. That is Victoria, four years old on the 1901 round and the only child they ever had.

A young household entirely new to the record: a box manufacturer of 29, his wife, a baby of nine months, and two servants - a cook and a nurse for the one child. Married two years, one child born and living.

**Margaret Dunn was born at Pittenweem in Fife** and is marked *Resident* rather than visitor, so she had come south for the work. 1901 held Joseph Youngman, a bank manager of 50, with his sister.

people.name: Fredk Harold Maden Eberlin
people.note: New to the record. It holds his brother **Albert Edgar (#1829), born 1895**, from the 1921 return - and the marriage answers here give two children born and two living, so the pair of them are the whole family.

households.note:
**The two servants are sisters.** Louisa and Nellie Wharmby, 23 and 18, both born at Underwood - a mining village north-west of the city - in service together in the same house. Neither is in the record.

The Eberlins are held at this house from the 1921 return; this puts them there ten years earlier. 1901 held William F. Bromley, stockbroker.

people.name: Elizabeth Helen Brewster
people.note: **British subject by parentage**, which the schedule states. The record already has her birthplace as Ostend from the 1891 return; the 1901 round I read gives only "Belgium".

people.name: Mary Allsebrook
people.note: **Still with her after ten years.** She is a cook in this house in 1901 at 25 and a lady's maid here at 38 - thirteen years of drift in ten, which is why the duplicate checks cannot pair the two rows.

households.note:
**John T. Brewster died between 1901 and 1911.** The record holds him at this house as a solicitor of 72 in 1901; here his widow keeps it alone at 76, with three servants and no family. Married twenty-nine years and **no children born to the marriage at all**, which the 1911 return states and nothing else could.

Four women in eleven rooms, one of them Belgian-born, and not one of them related to another.

people.name: Alfred Bradley
people.note: **#3504.** The record holds him at this house in 1891 and 1901; this is the third census of him here, and the trade is fuller than either - *cotton yarn* manufacturer, where 1891 gave only cotton doubler and 1901 retired cotton doubler.

people.name: Alice Margaret Gill
people.note: **#1817.** His niece, and she keeps house with him across three returns - 28 here in 1901, 38 now, and still in the record in 1921. Her birth year is consistent at 1873 in all three, which is rarer than it sounds.

households.note:
Thirteen rooms, five people, and a bachelor of 66 keeping house with his unmarried niece and three servants - the same arrangement the record holds here in 1891 and 1901.

**The Bradleys of Park Terrace are worth seeing together.** Charles at number 3 in 1891, Herbert a boarder at number 10 in 1891 and head of number 3 from 1901 to 1921, Alfred here at Broxtowe House across three censuses. Three men born 1842, 1846 and 1848, all in Nottingham, all on one short street. Almost certainly brothers, and nothing in the record says so.

None of the three servants is in the record, and none was born within forty miles.

people.name: Arundel Preston
people.note: **The sex on this schedule contradicts the record.** The age 73 is written in the FEMALES column and the condition is *widow*. But #4027 Arundel Preston is a man - head of this same house in 1901 at 63, a widower, "Gentleman" - and 63 to 73 is an exact ten years. Either the age went into the wrong column and *widow* is loose for widower, or his widow of the same name heads the house and he died in the decade. The family uses Arundel for a woman as well: his daughter is Arundel Aplin. Not resolved here.

households.note:
**Tisbury, Wiltshire** - the 1901 round gave only *Wiltshire*, so the town is new.

**And a generation the record has never held.** Arundel Aplin, a widowed daughter of 42, is here with two granddaughters, Alys Arundel and Alfreda Althea, 11 and 9. No Aplin is in the record at all. A widowed daughter come home with her children, in a house of thirteen rooms holding one man and seven women.

people.name: Elizabeth Christiana Wadsworth
people.note: **The record spells her Christine**; her husband writes **Christiana** here in his own hand. Her birthplace is Daybrook in the record and on this schedule; my reading of the 1901 round gave Basford, a mile or so away.

households.note:
**Three children born, two still living, one died.** The record holds two - Hope, here at 33, and John, a mechanical engineer of 25 on the 1901 round and not at home now. The third never reached the record at all, and nothing but this return would have said there was one.

Married thirty-nine years, so about 1872. The Wadsworths are at 31 Cavendish Road East by 1921, so this is the middle of three addresses.

people.name: Julius Meyrick
people.note: **Born in Saxony and a naturalised British subject**, the year given but only partly legible - it reads as about 18-something. A third German-born householder on the estate in 1911, beside Runge at 10 Park Terrace and the Flersheims on Pelham Crescent.

households.note: A widower of 70 alone with a cook and a housemaid in eight rooms. Nobody of this name is in the record. By 1921 the house is Charles Henry Vickers's, a lace manufacturer.

**Three unmarried brothers, all timber merchants, keeping house together** - the youngest the employer and the two elder his workers, which is the household's whole shape in one line. The record holds all three from the 1921 return and nothing earlier.

Their two servants are a married couple, a butler and a housekeeper, both from Lincolnshire and both 39. Four men and one woman in ten rooms.

people.name: Mary Enfield
people.note: **She is in the record twice and my import made the second.** #1871 (born 1842) carries her 1921 row; #4853 (born 1832) was created by the 1901 gap round, because I read her age there as 69. She is 69 HERE, ten years later - so one of the two readings is wrong, and the 1911 one agrees with the record. The 1901 age was very likely 59.

people.name: Jane Chaffer
people.note: **Entered as a VISITOR in 1901 and as a paid companion here.** Thirteen years in the same house, and the word for what she was changed rather than the arrangement.

households.note: Three women, none related, in seven rooms - a spinster of 69, her paid companion of 68, and a housemaid of 23.

The whole family is in the record from the 1921 return and nothing earlier; this gives them ten years sooner, with both boys at 7 and 5. He is a private tutor working **at home**, which the 1921 return calls tutor and examination coach.

A widow and her one servant. Neither is in the record: 1901 held Edmund Dalton, a bank clerk from Lincoln, with his wife, a visitor and a cook.

Married thirty-five years and widowed by 56, with one child born and living - who is not here.

**7 PARK VALLEY IS MELBROOK HOUSE.** The householder wrote *Melbrook House, Park* on the cover and A. Hagues has checked the enumerator's address section, which gives **7 Park Valley**. Both are the same house: the number is the official address, the name is what the family called it.

**The name is not in the record, and neither is any other on this street.** Not one of Park Valley's eighteen properties has an entry in the house-names table, where Peveril Drive has Parkdale and Peveril House and Hamilton Drive has Ferndene. This is the first, and it is worth adding to #263.

**And the same surname holds the house across the gap.** 1901 gives **Alfred Wilson, 81**, living on means with his widowed daughter Alice Lynam; 1911 gives **John Croshaw Wilson, 35**, a hosiery manufacturer. Forty-six years apart and the same name in the same house - grandfather and grandson would fit, and nothing here proves it.

**The children are entered after the servants**, which is the wrong order for a schedule and suggests they were remembered late. Marjorie and Vera both carry **Croshaw** as a middle name, which makes them unusually easy to trace.

people.name: Edna Blanche Wilson Ashworth
people.note: **The record has her as Edith B. W. Ashworth, born 1901**, from the 1901 round at Park Ravine. Same initials, same year: Edna read as Edith.

households.note:
**A Swiss governess.** Jean Band, 19, born at Geneva and returned as a Swiss subject - brought in for three children under eleven. The word was first written *Gouterness*, struck out and written again.

**And the fourth child is accounted for.** Four born alive, three still living, one died. The record holds **Leslie F. H. Ashworth, born 1900**, from the 1901 round; he is not in this house and not anywhere else in the record after it. He is very probably the one who died, and nothing but the 1911 marriage questions would have said there was a fourth child at all.

**Frederick John Ashworth is #4546** - the record has him at Park Ravine in 1901, where the variant check paired him wrongly with the Wadsworths. He is a timber importer of 38, and 9 Park Valley held Charles Cullen, a retired druggist of 89, ten years earlier.

people.name: Sarah Dawson
people.note: **Ninety-one, and exactly ten years older than the record has her in 1901.** Her age is the most consistent in this whole round.

people.name: Leonard Leslie Dawson
people.occupation: Clerk to a chartered accountant | Worker

households.note:
**A widow of 91 keeping house with two grandsons.** The record holds her here in 1891 beside her husband Alfred and in 1901 already widowed with grandsons Arthur and Percy. Percy has gone and a third grandson, Leonard Leslie of 19, has appeared.

**One child born alive and none still living** - so the grandsons' parent predeceased her, and the boys were raised by their grandmother. That is why they are in her house and not their own, and no other return says it.

households.postal_address_on_cover: Park Valley, Nottingham [the number reads as 12 or 13]

people.name: George Benedict Kohn
people.occupation: Lace merchant; export merchant; managing director
people.note: **Very probably #3017 Benedict Kohn, born 1858** - the son of the Kohn household at 11 Pelham Crescent on the 1901 round, whose head I read as *Richard* and who the record holds as Rocha, a widow. Fifty-three here gives 1858 exactly.

households.note:
**THIS HOUSEHOLD CANNOT BE FILED, BECAUSE THE RECORD HAS NO SUCH HOUSE.** Park Valley's properties run 1 to 11, then jump to 15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25 and Valley House. **There is no 12, 13 or 14.** A. Hagues read this as number 12; the postal address line reads as 12 or 13 and I cannot tell which.

Either the street once had houses the property list does not, or these numbers were later absorbed. Nothing is filed until that is settled, and the household is here rather than in the import file.

**The head is a Kohn, and the Kohns are already in the record.** George Benedict Kohn, 53, single, a lace and export merchant and a managing director, born at Beeston. The 1901 round puts a Kohn household at 11 Pelham Crescent - a widow of 67 born in Germany, a German subject, with sons Benedict, Herman and Charles and a daughter Fanny. Charles is a lecturer on chemistry. This is Benedict, ten years on and keeping his own house.

people.name: John Holland Walker
people.occupation: Department manager, wholesale clothing factory | Worker

households.note:
**John Holland Walker.** The name is worth stopping on: a J. Holland Walker of Nottingham wrote extensively on the town's history in the early twentieth century, including an itinerary of its streets published by the Thoroton Society. Whether that is this man - a department manager in a wholesale clothing factory, 37, born at Leeds - the record cannot settle on its own, but the name is uncommon enough to be worth the asking. See [[john-holland-walker]].

**Eleven years married and no children born**, which the 1911 return states. 15 Park Valley in 1901 held J. T. McCraith, a yarn agent, who is at 7 Park Terrace by this census.

**George Pearson, grocer and employer**, with his wife Emily and a son of 22 who is a **curtain designer** and himself an employer - two trades and two employers under one roof.

**Twenty-four years married, one child born alive, one still living** - and that one is Ernest, here at 22. An only child in a household of four.

**The record holds the couple in 1921 at 7 Park Valley**, where he is a land and property agent rather than a grocer. Fourteen doors and a change of trade, and the ages agree: he is 48 here and the record has him born 1863, she is 53 and the record has her born 1859.

people.name: Harriett Katherine Hackett
people.note: **The record has no middle name for her.** The schedule writes Katherine above the surname.

households.note:
**Harriett Hackett at 80, exactly ten years on from the 1901 round.** The record holds her here in 1891 and my reading of the 1901 round gives her at 70, living on own means, with two servants. Now 80, single, with one.

**And her middle name, which the record does not have.** The schedule writes **Katherine** above the surname - Harriett Katherine Hackett.

Two women in nine rooms, neither related to the other, one of them 80 and one 50.

**Martha Langham has died.** The record holds her here in 1891 and my reading of the 1901 round gives her at 58 beside her husband; he is a **widower** on this schedule. She died between 1901 and 1911, and a death registration would date it.

**And his birthplace is now a town.** The 1901 round gave only *Leicestershire*; this gives **Husbands Bosworth**.

**John Langham is in the record twice.** #4075, born 1834, carries his 1891 row; #4800, born 1841, was created by the 1901 gap-round import. Seventy-one here gives 1840, which is #4800's year. The pair wants merging - and it is why eight relationship blocks in the Park Valley file could not be made: *john langham* names two people, so the importer refuses them all.

**The son's birth year disagrees with itself.** The record has **Thomas C Langham born 1874** from 1891. The 1901 round gives him at 21 and this schedule at 31, which both make 1880. Two of three sources say 1880. There is also an elder son in the record, **John A Langham born 1868**, who is not in this house.

**A farmer living on The Park.** Thomas Cecil is a *master farmer* and an employer at 31, in a town house in the middle of Nottingham - so the farm was held at a distance and worked by other hands. His father is an iron merchant and an employer at 71, still trading.

people.name: James Calvert Wilson
people.note: **The industry column says NEWCASTLE ESTATE**, and the record has only "Land surveyor". See [[newcastle-estate-surveyor]].

people.name: Florence Gertrude Watkins
people.note: **The record has her surname as Wathing.** The schedule reads Watkins.

people.name: Donald Hickling Richardson
people.occupation: Bank clerk, United Counties Banking Co | Worker

households.note:
**ALREADY IN THE RECORD** - all seven, from the 1911 spreadsheet. Nothing here is new except what the columns beside the names say, and two of those matter.

**James Calvert Wilson is land surveyor to the NEWCASTLE ESTATE.** The record has the trade and not the employer, and the employer is the point: the Duke of Newcastle's estate is The Park. This is the man who surveyed the ground this whole record is about. See [[newcastle-estate-surveyor]].

**The servant's surname is Watkins, not Wathing**, and Wathing is not a surname at all.

**And the family came from Yorkshire by way of Lancashire.** Both parents born at Huddersfield, both daughters at Burnley, and the family in Nottingham by 1911 - twenty-five years of marriage and three children, all living.

households.postal_address_on_cover: Clare Valley, Nottingham - NO house name or number
households.note:
**ALREADY IN THE RECORD at Ribble Lodge (#65)**, from the 1911 spreadsheet - which is worth noting, because **this schedule gives no house name and no number at all**, only *Clare Valley*. So the record's placement at Ribble Lodge came from some other source, and this return neither confirms nor contradicts it.

Married two years and no children. A lace manufacturer of 41 and his wife, with one servant of fifteen.

**Two managers of wallpaper manufacturers under one roof** - Richard Kirby, who heads the house, and Harry Wilbourn Gregory, a visitor of 32 with exactly the same trade in exactly the same industry. Colleagues staying the night, on census night, is the likeliest reading, and it is the sort of thing only a return catches.

**The record holds the Kirbys from 1921 and not before.** This puts them at the house ten years earlier, and adds a son, Richard, aged 4 and born at Derby - so the family came from Derby between 1907 and 1911. He is not in the 1921 household, which by then holds a visiting sister instead.

**The nursemaid is fourteen.** Annie Rodgers, in service and returned as a worker, born at Stanley in Derbyshire. Every servant in this house is Derbyshire-born and the family is London-born, which is the pattern the whole estate shows: the households come from anywhere, the people who wait on them come from the next county.

**Two marriages are answered on this schedule**, the Gregorys' as well as the Kirbys' - married two years, no children. That is unusual: a visitor's marriage is normally left blank.

marriage.note: She is a widow, so the years-married column is left blank.

people.name: Christopher Harold Weller
people.occupation: Clerk in holy orders, Church of England - St Mary's, Nottingham | Worker

people.name: Frank Gilbert Weller
people.occupation: Colliery manager's pupil, Butterley Company | Worker

people.name: Rose Adelaide Macaulay
people.occupation: High school mistress (retired), Notting Hill High School | Worker

households.note:
**A curate of St Mary's keeping house for his widowed mother and his younger brother.** Christopher Harold Weller is 31 and in holy orders at the town's principal church; his brother Frank Gilbert, 21, is a **colliery manager's pupil with the Butterley Company** - an apprenticeship into the Derbyshire coal and iron trade, and about as far from the pulpit as two brothers can get.

**Their mother bore twelve children and buried two.** Edith Weller, widow, 59, born at Chesham: twelve born alive, ten still living. Two of her sons are in this house and the other eight children are elsewhere. Nothing but a 1911 return states a family of that size.

**And the servant has eight children of her own, all living.** Annie Worthington, a widow of 50, in general service. Her marriage columns are filled in beside her mistress's, which is rare - a servant's answers are usually left blank - and the two women's lives sit side by side on the page: twelve children and a house of nine rooms, eight children and a place in it.

**The visitor is a retired high school mistress** of Notting Hill High School, one of the Girls' Public Day School Trust's foundations, born at Camden Town. **She is not the novelist Rose Macaulay**, who was born in 1881 and would be thirty here; this Rose Adelaide was born about 1849. The names are close enough that somebody will one day assume otherwise, which is why it is written down.

**The whole household is new to the record.** 2 Clare Valley holds nothing before 1921, when it is the Shepherds'.

marriage.note: A widow, so the years-married column is left blank.

households.note:
**ALREADY IN THE RECORD** from the 1911 spreadsheet, and nothing here is new - but the schedule raises a question about the record's own Wilkins girls.

**LAWRENCE WILKINS HAS DIED.** The record holds him here in 1901 as a clergyman of 39; his widow heads the house at 41. He died between 1901 and 1911.

**Four children born, four still living** - and three are here. The fourth is **L. A. Wilkins, a son of 6 in 1901**, who would be 16 and is absent. Away at school is the likeliest reason.

**But the two elder daughters may be in the record twice under different names.** 1901 gives **Eleanor born 1896** and **Jessie born 1897**; 1911 gives **Joyce born 1896** and **Mary born 1897**. Same house, same mother, same birth years, four separate records. Either the girls have forenames the two sources chose differently between, or one reading is wrong. The 1911 names are in their mother's own hand, which is the better authority. See [[wilkins-girls-named-twice]].

**The two servants are sisters**, Ellen and Edith Mansfield, both from Woodville in Staffordshire - the second pair of sisters in service the 1911 round has turned up, after the Wharmbys at 16 Park Terrace.

households.postal_address_on_cover: Clare Valley Lodge, The Park, Nottingham
households.note:
**CLARE VALLEY LODGE IS NOT IN THE PROPERTY LIST, AND IT EXPLAINS AN UNFILED 1901 HOUSEHOLD.** The record's Clare Valley holds 1 to 5, 15, Grove House, Ribble Lodge, Springdale and The Spinney. There is no Lodge.

**But the 1901 round already found one.** George Hill, a Baptist minister of 53, with his wife and six children, is parked unfiled under *Lodge, Clare Valley (no house of that name in the record)*. This schedule names the house outright, from the householder's own hand, ten years later. **The Lodge is real and the Hill household belongs to it.**

**The house is not filed here either**, because naming a house is not the same as knowing which property it is - and the record has no property to file it to. It wants creating. See [[clare-valley-missing-houses]].

Fourteen rooms, seven people: a retired lace manufacturer, his wife, a daughter of 28 and two sons - a bank clerk and a chartered accountant, both still at home at 27 and 22. Twenty-nine years married, three children born, three living, and all three under this roof.

**ELMSDALE IS 5 CLARE VALLEY** - #63, placed by A. Hagues from the ground: the corner house, huge, and semi-detached with number 4. The record describes #62 and #63 in exactly those words, *semi-detached, c1890, part of a group of five facing the southern end of the Bowl*.

**Emma Elizabeth Goddard, 65, a widow on private means, with one servant.** She is already in the record at this house for **1921**, aged 76, with a servant called Lily Dran - so her 1911 and 1921 returns now sit together, and the placing is confirmed by the record rather than resting on the reading of a cover.

**Placing it moved seventeen census rows, not two.** Arthur Lewis the iron merchant and his family have been unfiled since the 1891 round under *Elmsdale (Clare Valley / Tattershall Drive, by Wright's Directory)* - eight rows for 1891 and seven for 1901, because the directory named two streets and nobody could tell which was meant. **5 Clare Valley now holds a continuous line through 1891, 1901, 1911 and 1921**, where before it held only 1921.

**Her coachman may be findable too.** Goddards Lodge on Tattershall Drive holds John Newham, coachman, in 1911 - and A. Hagues notes a possible lodge at the front of this house. If that is the same building, the directory's two streets were right twice. See [[clare-valley-missing-houses]].

**THE POSTMASTER OF NOTTINGHAM.** William Vincent Harnett, 62, gives his occupation in those words and his employer as the Post Office - a public office of real standing in the town, and nobody of the name is in the record.

**His career is written in his children's birthplaces.** Born at Blackfriars, married at 29 years to a woman born in St John's Wood; eldest daughter born at Richmond in Surrey, second at Hammersmith, and the family in Nottingham by 1911. A Post Office man moved where the service sent him, and the moves are datable from the girls' ages.

**Three children born, two still living.** The one who died is not otherwise traceable.

**St Ives is 4 Tattershall Drive** - #309, confirmed by A. Hagues. The record holds the name already, in the property's history text, and Dougal de Havilland's Park Map labels the plot **4StIves**, which is how T C Hine was accepted as its architect. See [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

people.name: Martha Stubbs
people.note: surname hard to read - Stubbs or Stubber

households.note:
**A house of three women and no men at all** - a widow of 67 on private means and her two servants. One of very few all-female households in the 1911 round.

**Lynwood is 2 Tattershall Drive** - #307, confirmed by A. Hagues, and the record already carries the name in the property's history text. The same entry suggests **Lawrence Bright, the architect of much of Huntingdon Drive, may himself have lived here c1900-1910** - and this schedule says he did not, or at least not in April 1911. Janet Griggs is not in the record.

See [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

**Newly married** - the marriage column reads *under one year*, so Robert Hutchinson, a corn miller employing others, and Joyce, ten years his junior and born at Reading, had been married a matter of months on census night.

**The two servants are sisters.** Ellen Capps, 41, cook, and Sarah Capps, 37, housemaid, both born at Kineton in Warwickshire - a village 60 miles off, which two sisters reached together. **No Capps of any kind is in the record**, and a pair arriving in service as a pair is worth noticing: it usually means a place got through family rather than an agency.

**Twelve Hutchinsons are already in the record and none of them is this Robert** - the one Robert Hutchinson held, #3172, was born 1831.

**ROY HENDERSON THE BARITONE, AGED 11, AT HOME.** The record's own description of #310 already says the house *was once occupied by Roy Henderson (1899-2000), popular English baritone in the 1920s, 30s and 40s* - but held no evidence for it and not one member of the family. **This schedule is that evidence**: Roy Galbraith Henderson, son, 11, at school, born Edinburgh, in his father's own hand. See [[roy-henderson-baritone-at-5-tattershall]].

**His father is the reason the family is in Nottingham.** Alexander Roy Henderson, 48, Congregational church minister, born at King Edward in Aberdeenshire.

**The children's birthplaces date every move.** Married 19 years; eldest born Montrose, the next two Edinburgh, the youngest Nottingham - so the family came south between Roy's birth in 1899 and Kenneth's in 1906 or 1907.

**Four children born, four living** - no loss in this house, which is uncommon in the round.

**The whole household is new.** The record holds one Henderson, Caroline Hannah, and she is not of this family.

households.postal_address_on_cover: Goddards Lodge, Tattershall Drive, The Park
households.note:
**A COACHMAN'S LODGE, AND IT NAMES THE FAMILY IT SERVED.** John Newham, 44, coachman, and his wife, in five rooms. The house is *Goddards Lodge* - and three weeks of transcription earlier in this round put **Emma Elizabeth Goddard, 65, at Elmsdale on Clare Valley**.

**That pairing looks like the answer to a long-standing problem.** Arthur Lewis and his family sit unfiled for both 1891 and 1901 under *Elmsdale (Clare Valley / Tattershall Drive, by Wright's Directory)* - and nobody could tell which street the house was on, because the directory gave both. **If the house stands on Clare Valley and its lodge on Tattershall Drive, the directory was right twice.** The grounds run between the two roads, as they do at 2 and 4 Tattershall Drive, whose gardens reach Huntingdon Drive. Not proved, but it fits the ground.

**Emma Elizabeth Goddard is already in the record**, #1951, born 1845, filed at property 63 in 1921 - so she is traceable, and the 1921 return may name the house.

**Married 22 years and no children born at all** - unusual enough in this round to be worth a note.

**Not filed.** See [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

people.name: William Henry Holmes
people.occupation: Representative, maltsters, malt extract manufacturers and yeast merchants | worker

households.note:
**THE COVER GIVES NO NUMBER** - just *Tattershall Drive, The Park, Nottingham*. This one cannot be filed from the schedule alone, and wants the enumerator's address column. **Do not guess it**; the neighbours on either side in the enumerator's running order will settle it.

**Two generations and the smallest house on the street so far** - six rooms, against nine, ten and eleven at Lynwood, 3 and 5. A man of 41 keeping his elderly parents, rather than a household with servants; there are none here.

**All four were born at Radford**, and the family has not moved far.

**Married 49 years, one child born alive, one still living** - and that one child is the head of the house. William and Sarah Ann Holmes had a single son in half a century of marriage, and were living with him at the end of it.

**William Henry's trade is worth a look.** *Representative* to maltsters, malt extract manufacturers and yeast merchants - a commercial traveller in the brewing supply trade, and his father a retired licensed victualler. **The son sold to the trade his father had worked in.**

**Not filed** - needs the number.

**FOUR ROOMS, A BARMAN AND A LODGER** - and nothing else in the 1911 round looks like it. Walter William Jackson works behind the bar of a public house; his wife and small daughter are with him; and they let a room to **George William Knott, 57, a widowed piano maker from London**.

**This is a working household on a wealthy estate.** Every other Tattershall Drive schedule so far has nine, ten or eleven rooms and servants living in. This one has four rooms and takes in a boarder to help pay for them. **The Park held both, side by side, and the record should show that.**

**A piano maker is an unusual trade for the record** and worth its own look - Nottingham had the trade, and a London-trained man of 57 boarding here had a working life behind him.

**The cover gives no number** - the second Tattershall Drive schedule in a row that does not. See [[tattershall-drive-unnumbered-households]]. **Not filed.**

**ALREADY IN THE RECORD, AND STUCK IN THE SAME PLACE TEN YEARS LATER.** All three Lilleys are held from the **1921** census - #2278, #2279, #2280 - and all three are **unfiled there too**, under the bare unresolved address *Tattershall Drive*. The 1911 cover gives no number either. **The same house has defeated two rounds.**

**Ages agree exactly**: Walter 40 in 1911 against born 1870; Annie 43 against 1867; Doris 8 against 1903.

**He changed trade between the two censuses.** Hairdresser's assistant in 1911, **chiropodist** by 1921 - the record has it as *Chirpidist*, which wants correcting. It is a natural move rather than a strange one; barbers had long done feet as well as hair.

**The daughter's middle name disagrees.** This schedule, in her father's hand, reads **Doris May**. The record has her as **Doris Mary**. One of the two is wrong and the 1911 schedule is the better authority, being the householder's own writing.

**Four rooms, no servants** - the third such household on Tattershall Drive in this round. See [[tattershall-drive-unnumbered-households]].

**A WOMAN RUNNING A FACTORY.** Alice Marron, 38, widow, gives her occupation as **cardboard box manufacturer** and answers the employer column **Employer** - not worker, not own account. She employed people.

**That is rare in this record and rare in the 1911 census generally.** Women heading households in The Park are overwhelmingly widows on private means; a widow running a manufacturing business, with a boy of ten and four rooms, is a different life entirely. **She is worth her own research.** See [[alice-marron-box-manufacturer]].

**Born at Poplar in London** - so she came to Nottingham, and the business may have come with her or been her late husband's. **The son's birth at Nottingham about 1901 dates her arrival** to before that.

**No Marron of any kind is in the record.**

**And there is no 5 North Road in the property list** - it holds 2, 4, 6, 7 and 8. Number 4, #412, was itself added as a census-only property, which is the route this one should take. **Not filed.**
